If you know the course and its topics, you can have a deep understanding of linear algebra using this book. However, the book is so complicated that you cannot learn from the textbook. Moreover, the syllabus of the course does not match with the textbook in the syllabus. Then, the topics are not covered in a queue, so if you want to use the book for self-study, you again cannot because the textbook requires foreknowledge about the topic you have covered in the second week. These situations make the course harder than it is. Furthermore, I do not understand how a course about vectors can be covered without drawing a plane or a vector. All of the equations, logic and signs in the course are related to the vectors, planes and spaces. However,  the main theme of the course is not related to the real world. The course focuses on proving equations and relations without describing how to reach them using the basics of vectors. Even though you work hard and you attend all the classes, it is impossible to feel comfortable and confident about the subjects. There are better textbooks and better approaches to teaching linear algebra rather than teaching mathematical sentences without telling where they come from. I recommend Gilbert Strang`s approach for this course. Reading his book, which the library has, and watching his YouTube videos, recorded in 2005,  are better for learning linear algebra than attending the class the whole semester. Although you cannot learn all the equations and mathematical expressions, you can learn how, why and when an operation is used, which, I believe, is the important part of knowing something.

When I first encountered deep mathematics, I thought it was gibberish. Why were we proving addition? It seemed intuitively obvious—if you add a set containing two distinct apples to another set of two distinct apples, you get a set with four apples. "This is nonsense," I thought. But the week before finals, I finally understood: intuitive logic breaks down when dealing with concepts like infinity and paradoxes. Consider statements like "this statement is false" or "a catalog that contains all catalogs that don't contain themselves." Once I truly grasped these contradictions, I could finally begin to understand abstract mathematics. It opened up a world of deep concepts: mathematical induction, deductive proofs, and the paradoxes of calculus—from infinite volume spheres to Lewis Carroll's geometry riddles, Galileo's paradox, and Aristotle's contradiction. The concept of infinity, Cantor's works, the Liar paradox, the Barber paradox, Russell's paradox, and even axiomatic set theory and abelian groups all began to make sense. Unfortunately, despite the instructor's efforts, they failed to convey this fascinating depth of mathematics to the class.
